    Auditing Unequal Random-Intercept Calibration

    random-intercept-calibration-audit.Rmd

    The Phase 11 pinned run produced a 7.6% Monte Carlo null-rejection rate in one 500-dataset batch. That result is not enough to distinguish an engine defect from ordinary between-batch variation. Phase 14 audits the randomization test against exact unique treatment assignments and genuinely independent seed batches.

    Two permutation spaces

    With four clusters in each of three size strata, there are (4!)^3 = 13,824 rearrangements of distinct cluster profiles. If two clusters per stratum are control and two are impact, there are only choose(4, 2)^3 = 216 unique treatment-label assignments. Rearrangements that only swap two profiles occupying the same treatment positions give duplicate test statistics. Exact p-values from the two spaces must agree.

    The Phase 11 reduced model is intercept only. For any whole-cluster permutation matrix (P), its Freedman–Lane transformation is

    H0+P(I−H0)=P, H_0 + P(I-H_0) = P,

    because a permutation leaves the intercept unchanged. Thus the implemented residual permutation is algebraically the raw conditional randomization test, not an approximation to it.

    Executable audit

    This small run exercises every audit path while keeping vignette build time short:

    audit_smoke <- audit_unequal_random_intercept_calibration(
  batches = 2,
  simulations_per_batch = 25,
  permutations = 19,
  engine_checks = 2,
  seed = 20260719
)
audit_smoke

    The full release-record audit is:

    audit <- audit_unequal_random_intercept_calibration(
  batches = 20,
  simulations_per_batch = 500,
  permutations = 99,
  engine_checks = 10,
  seed = 20260719
)

    Across 10,000 datasets per valid scenario, exact/Monte Carlo rejection was 4.76%/4.83% for the Gaussian balanced allocation, 4.58%/4.95% for unequal within-size treatment allocation, and 4.53%/4.42% under heavy-tailed random effects and residuals. Full distance-engine F statistics matched the unique assignment calculation within 8.9e-16; exact p-values were identical.

    Why adjacent seeds are not independent batches

    The validation functions assign a deterministic seed to each simulation. Two audits started from adjacent base seeds would therefore reuse nearly every per-iteration seed, producing almost identical rejection rates. The Phase 14 audit prevents that mistake by spacing batch seeds one million apart and recording the complete seed design.

    The dispersion-violation scenario is labelled as a sensitivity analysis. It deliberately changes residual variance by treatment and therefore does not satisfy the exchangeability null; it is never used to pass or fail the nominal calibration gate.
